![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/562596b4267c6a13ef13c4f20e7861b00675e85febc43653efd141d720900804.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above. Given that $f(0)=0,$ which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points: 

$\,$ $x=-1\,$ and $\,x=0.$

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{not extr.}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical lines $x=-1,$ and $x=0.$

- Since we are told that $f(0)=0,$ we can draw that point on the graph.

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-1,0)$, the point at $x=0$ must be lower than the point at $x=-1.$

So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/504a1af2c6d97200a3b211e8a7c67298082cd3cffbf866851afa63f7162dcce3.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-1)$ and on $(-1,0)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left and down to the right of $x=-1.$

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-1,0)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(0,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/6e6c1b9806b3dbf340255884722429a67dc3a7cd55d8cc0a0bbeeb48dcae1c87.png)

- Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/10185719d14812cd4f58a592f106fe4fd81540ab6f6177f61d77bd6ec4e5d6c4.png)
